segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Listen to a talk on a social science podcast.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Today, we're exploring a fascinating concept in social psychology known as pluralistic ignorance.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Pluralistic ignorance describes a situation where the majority of members in a group privately reject a norm or standard, but assume incorrectly that most others accept it.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: This often results in everyone conforming to a norm they don't truly agree with.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: A classic example occurs in workplace overtime culture.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Many employees might prefer to leave work on time, but they stay late because they believe everyone else is committed to working extra hours.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: In reality, most colleagues also wish to leave on time, but fear appearing less dedicated.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: When employees are asked privately about their preferences, many express a desire for better work-life balance.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Despite their public behavior suggesting enthusiasm for long hours.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Pluralistic ignorance has broad implications well beyond the workplace.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Notably, it can perpetuate social stereotypes and hinder societal change as individuals might hesitate to voice dissenting opinions thinking they're in the minority.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: However, overcoming pluralistic ignorance has powerful benefits.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: When even one person speaks up, it can embolden others to express their true beliefs, potentially leading to a shift in group norms and to more honest, authentic communities.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: But there's a challenge, and it's a big one.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Being the first to speak out often requires courage, as it can risk one's social standing among one's peers.
